title: More Than Just Data
body:
My journey into data analytics has been one of continuous learning, curiosity, and discovery. What started with an academic foundation in Geoinformatics gradually evolved into a deeper interest in understanding data, uncovering patterns, and turning information into meaningful insights.

Over time, I've come to realize that working with data is about much more than writing queries, building dashboards, or automating processes. It's about asking the right questions, understanding the problem behind the numbers, and finding ways to make information useful.

Throughout my journey, I've learned a few lessons that continue to shape the way I approach my work:

- Curiosity is essential. 
Never be afraid to ask why something looks the way it does. Sometimes the most valuable insights come from questioning what others take for granted.

There is always more than one way to solve a problem. The first solution isn't necessarily the best one. Exploring alternatives often leads to more efficient and sustainable approaches.

- Understand the data before analysing it. 
A beautiful dashboard means very little if the underlying data isn't reliable or the business context isn't understood.

- Never stop learning. 
Technology evolves, tools change, and new challenges emerge. Staying curious and adaptable is part of becoming a better analyst.

- Don't underestimate the basics. 
Some of the most effective solutions aren't necessarily the most complicated ones.

One thing I've particularly come to appreciate is that growth doesn't always happen through major projects or significant milestones. Sometimes it's found in debugging a stubborn piece of code, simplifying a complicated process, or discovering a better way to approach an everyday task.

I'm still learning, still experimenting, and still finding new ways to approach problems. If there's one thing this journey has taught me, it's that becoming a better data analyst is less about knowing everything and more about being willing to learn something new every day.

And this is only the beginning.

title: Five SQL habits that save me time
body:
When working with data, efficiency isn't always about writing more complex queries. Sometimes, it's about developing better habits that make your work cleaner, faster, and easier to maintain.

Over time, I've found that a few simple SQL practices can make a noticeable difference in everyday analysis. Here are five habits worth adopting.

## Avoid "SELECT *" whenever possible.

It's tempting to retrieve every column using SELECT *, especially when exploring a new dataset. However, selecting only the columns you need makes queries more intentional, reduces unnecessary data retrieval, and makes your code easier to understand.

```sql
SELECT
    ProductName,
    Brand,
    Category
FROM Products;
```

## Use Meaningful Aliases.

Give your tables and calculated columns descriptive aliases. This makes complex queries involving multiple joins much easier to read and maintain.

```sql
SELECT
    p.ProductName,
    s.SalesAmount
FROM Products AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales AS s
    ON p.ProductID = s.ProductID;
```

## Filter Data as Early as Possible.

Use WHERE conditions to narrow down your dataset before performing unnecessary operations. Working with fewer records can improve query performance, particularly when dealing with large tables.

```sql
SELECT
    ProductID,
    SalesAmount
FROM Sales
WHERE SalesAmount > 1000;
```

## Use CTEs to Organise Complex Queries.

Common Table Expressions (CTEs) help break complicated queries into smaller, logical sections. Instead of writing one lengthy query, you can structure your analysis into manageable steps.

```sql
WITH MonthlySales AS (
    SELECT
        Month,
        SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY Month
)
SELECT *
FROM MonthlySales;
```

## Comment on Your Logic.

A query might make perfect sense today, but revisiting it several weeks later can be a different story. Brief comments explaining important calculations, business rules, or unusual filters can save you time when debugging or updating your work.

- Calculate total sales per product

```sql
SELECT
    ProductID,
    SUM(SalesAmount) AS TotalSales
FROM Sales
GROUP BY ProductID;
```

Final Thoughts.

Good SQL isn't just about getting the correct result. It's also about writing queries that are efficient, readable, and easy to maintain.

These habits may seem small, but consistently applying them can make everyday data analysis considerably smoother.

Write smarter, not just more SQL.
